source_document.body:
Great on any Friday: NOCO Boost+Air AX65 - 2000A Jump Starter & Tire Inflator
Unrestored Mustang Needs a Home, It Doesn't Even Need a Complete Restoration
26 photos
Photo: eBay seller mustangbecky
Say what you want about the 1965 Mustang , but everybody knows what this car eventually represented in the American car space. This specimen is here to remind us of this, and more importantly, it does it in an unrestored condition.
This means that the Mustang you see in these pics has never been altered or restored, so most of the things you’ll end up discovering were last touched by Ford ’s engineers back in the day when it was still on the assembly line.
The car’s number one priority is to find a new home, with a small refresh then required to shine again as it did on day one. More importantly, a full restoration is not necessary in this case, and based on the photos and the data shared by the owner, overhauling this Mustang shouldn’t be too difficult.
Photo: eBay seller mustangbecky I’m pretty sure everybody remembers how the Mustang came to be, but one thing I want to highlight is that this car was never supposed to be expensive. Lee Iaccocca wanted the Mustang to cost only $2,500, and the final production model got even better than that.
The 6-cylinder hardtop coupe – the model that people aren’t necessarily interested in these days – could be had for only $2,320. It was an affordable price for people who wanted a daily driver, and the six-powered Mustang was certainly up to the task. The original 170ci engine offered on the 1964 1/2 models delivered only 101 horsepower, as its focus was specifically on offering an efficient ride.
The convertible carried a starting price tag of $2,557, while the 2+2 fastback rolled out with a similar price tag - $2,553 – in September.
Ford knew that not everybody wanted an efficient ride, as the muscle under the hood was still a big thing back then. That’s why it launched a high-performance 289 rated at 271 horsepower in June 1964.
However, most people decided to stick with the base V8s – originally, this was a 260 with 164 horsepower, but when the 1965 model year stepped in, it was upgraded to a 289. A four-barrel version of the same engine was also offered.
Photo: eBay seller mustangbecky While a Hi-Po would have been a fantastic engine on this Mustang, especially considering it has never been restored, that’s not what you’ll find under its hood.
It still has a V8, but a regular 289 paired with an automatic transmission. It starts, runs, drives, you name it, and considering the car has never been restored, it should be safe to assume that this engine has never been rebuilt either.
I would still ask my mechanic to inspect what happens under the hood before anything else, as I don’t think that getting a 1965 Mustang without the original engine under the hood would make sense if the price weren’t the right one.
Otherwise, this Mustang certainly looks like a small piece of automotive history. It still wears the factory paint, and despite showing its age, with some obvious cracks that might be easier to notice during an in-person inspection, it’s still in good shape.
I wish we knew more about this Mustang because the condition of the paint and the unrestored shape suggest that the car has been babied throughout its entire life, and I wouldn’t be surprised to learn that it’s a family-owned specimen. Just ask all these questions during your live inspection because you could end up coming across quite a gem.
The interior is also in good shape and also original.
Photo: eBay seller mustangbecky The cabin also shows its age, but I think this is something we can ignore, considering it has never been refreshed. The car comes with air conditioning – still blowing cold – and power steering.
The rust isn’t a concern on this Mustang, and the owner says the car is as clean as possible. If possible, you should raise it on a lift and inspect the undersides because an unrestored pile of metal born in 1965 is very unlikely to escape without at least surface corrosion.
Otherwise, I expect this Mustang to find a new home quite fast if – and this is a big if – it's priced correctly.
Photo: eBay seller mustangbecky The owner believes that $18,500 is a fair expectation for an unrestored Mustang, but they also enabled the Make Offer option on eBay. This is an opportunity to discuss the price if you are committed to a purchase, and considering 21 people have already added the vehicle to their watchlists, you might some competition this time.
The listing is set to expire in 19 days, unless someone clicks the Buy It Now button earlier. Otherwise, if you want to see this Mustang in person, you must call the seller and then pack your bags for a trip to Dumas, Arkansas.
Considering its shape, it should be able to move on its own, so you won’t need to pay for shipping to your garage, especially if you don’t live far from this location.
